summary: Specifies a standard form for sending internationalized text across networks, much as ASCII was used in the early ARPANET. It uses UTF-8 with normalization and specific line-ending sequences. It replaces RFC 698. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Computers need an agreed way to write text in all languages. This paper picks one way to spell letters and end lines so everyone reads the same thing.

questions: utf-8 normalization line endings network text
why do internet protocols use crlf
what line ending does utf-8 network text use
subtitle: A standard way to send text in any language across the network: UTF-8, normalized, with CRLF line endings.

tldr.problem: Early Internet protocols assumed text meant ASCII in a standard Network Virtual Terminal form. Now that text is international, 'use Unicode' leaves open which encoding, which line endings and which normalization.
tldr.mechanism: Net-Unicode requires UTF-8, CRLF line endings, no C1 control characters, no byte order mark, no unassigned code points, and (SHOULD) Unicode normalization form NFC before sending.
tldr.outcome: It gives new protocols one stable reference for network text, the way NVT ASCII did for ASCII. It obsoletes RFC 698 and updates RFC 854.

today: RFC 5198 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 698 and updates RFC 854, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Network Text Needs a Standard
sections.content:
Historically, Internet protocols have been largely ASCII-based. When a protocol said 'text', it meant text in Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) or 'Network ASCII' form. Text is no longer just ASCII, and while the world is converging on Unicode, 'use Unicode' is more ambiguous than 'use ASCII' ever was.

Unicode gives each character an integer code point in the range 0-0x10ffff. Those integers can be turned into bytes in several encoding forms: UTF-8 (variable length), UTF-16 (16-bit units with surrogates for larger code points) and UTF-32 (a 32-bit integer per code point). On top of that, any of them can be combined with different line-ending conventions.

RFC 5198 proposes Net-Unicode as the standardized text transmission form for the Internet, an internationalized alternative to NVT ASCII for new and updated protocols. UTF-8 is chosen because of its compatibility with ASCII and the reasons in the IETF character set policy, RFC 2277. Whenever there is a choice, Unicode SHOULD be used with this encoding.
sections.eli5: Before, everyone used one alphabet for the network. Now there are many alphabets, so we need to agree on one way to write them all down.

sections.title: The Net-Unicode Rules
sections.content:
Section 2 of the RFC lists six rules. Parts of the definition are deliberately informal, giving guidance for protocols that reference it.

  • Characters MUST be encoded in UTF-8 as defined in RFC 3629.
  • If the protocol has lines, a line ending MUST be CR LF (U+000D then U+000A). CR SHOULD NOT appear except when followed by LF; the only other permitted context is CR NUL, which is not recommended.
  • ASCII-range control characters (U+0000 to U+001F and U+007F to U+009F) SHOULD generally be avoided. Space, CR, LF and Form Feed (U+000C) are exceptions, but FF needs care because it has no universal meaning. The C1 controls (U+0080 through U+009F) MUST NOT appear.
  • Text SHOULD be normalized to Unicode normalization form NFC before transmission.
  • The Byte Order Mark MUST NOT appear at the start of these strings.
  • Systems MUST NOT transmit any code point that is unassigned in the Unicode version they depend on, and the versions of NFC and Unicode used MUST be consistent.

The RFC says lines end in CRLF and only in CRLF. Anything that does not end in CRLF is either not a line or is severely malformed. The newer line-separator characters (IND, NEL, U+2028, U+2029) MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: The rules are like a school handwriting rule: use this one alphabet code, end every line the same way, and do not use weird special marks.

sections.title: Normalization with NFC
sections.content:
Some different strings of Unicode are canonically equivalent: they represent the same text. The RFC gives examples such as U+2126 OHM SIGN and U+03A9 GREEK CAPITAL LETTER OMEGA, or U+0061 followed by U+0300 COMBINING GRAVE ACCENT versus the single character U+00E0.

Comparing strings is far easier if equivalent text always has one unique form. The Unicode normalization form NFC maps canonically equivalent sequences to a single form, typically producing precomposed characters and putting other combining marks in a unique order. The RFC picks NFC because it is closest to actual use in practice, has the fewest side effects of treating different characters as equivalent, and usually needs the least work when converting from non-Unicode encodings.

Senders should normalize, but receivers should be prepared to receive unnormalized strings and not react to that in excessive ways. This follows the robustness principle and recognizes that applications may rely on operating system libraries they do not control.
sections.eli5: An accented letter can be written as one piece or as a letter plus a separate accent. NFC says to always glue them together the same way, so two identical words really look identical to a computer.

sections.title: Unicode Versions and Stability
sections.content:
Unicode grows over time, adding scripts and characters. The RFC argues that new versions should not significantly affect this format: mapping code points to UTF-8 is algorithmic and does not depend on whether a code point is assigned, and NFC makes a much more limited set of mappings than NFKC. The Unicode Consortium has guaranteed that a string with no unassigned characters that is NFC-normalized stays normalized in all future versions.

That is why Net-Unicode forbids unassigned code points: an unassigned code point normalizes to itself, but if it is assigned later it might take part in some other mapping. Private-use code points have no standard definitions and SHOULD be avoided.

The specification applies to Unicode version 5.0 up to, but not including, any version that changes the UTF-8 definition or NFC stability. Because applications usually rely on libraries that can change underneath them, the RFC lists four theoretical ways around the problem (freeze a version, add a version indicator, devise new normalization rules, or a 'Stable NFC' that rejects unassigned code points) and calls the fourth a reasonable compromise.
sections.eli5: New letters get added to the alphabet over time. The rules are written so that adding new letters will not break old messages, as long as nobody uses letters that do not exist yet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most security issues of UTF-8 in RFC 3629 apply here, though Net-Unicode should be slightly less exposed because it requires NFC and is somewhat more restrictive. Shifts in Unicode versions may introduce other issues.

Programs that receive these streams should use extreme caution about assuming that incoming data is normalized. Unnormalized forms and invalid UTF-8 could be part of an attack; for example, an attacker may deliberately send unnormalized text to avoid detection by naive text-matching systems such as firewalls.

The CR rule from NVT is repeated: CR must be followed by LF or NUL. NUL can be a trap in programming languages that use it as a string terminator, which is one more reason to avoid CR except in CRLF.
sections.eli5: A sneaky sender could write the same word in a different hidden way to slip past a guard who only looks for one spelling. Receivers should not assume everything is neatly spelled.

sections.title: History and the Line-Ending Problem
sections.content:
The appendices explain the context. Early ARPANET hosts used different character codes (BCD, EBCDIC and ASCII), and the Network Working Group chose ASCII as the standard, as '7-bit ASCII in an 8-bit field'. The Telnet protocol then established the Network Virtual Terminal, whose coding is variously called Telnet ASCII, NVT ASCII or network ASCII, with CRLF as the line ending. Telnet, FTP, SMTP, finger and whois are classic users of this model.

The RFC also reviews the NVT control characters, advising that BEL, BS, HT, VT and FF not be used except in exceptional circumstances, and that a bare LF or HT is problematic. It notes that if starting today it would probably be sensible to use LS (U+2028) exclusively, but the installed base of CRLF and compatibility with NVT make that impossible.

Appendix D suggests future work: a Telnet or SSH option for this type of stream and an FTP extension for a 'Unicode text' data type.
sections.eli5: The network has always agreed on one way to write text and end a line. Changing the line ending now would break too many old programs, so the new rules keep it.
